intro: Colchester, in Essex, has two readers' trees on our map, a couple of hundred metres apart near Clingoe Hill in Greenstead, on the east side of the town. One is a huge pedunculate oak standing alone in open grass, its short wide trunk hollowed and burred, which the Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory knows as the Wivenhoe Whopper and measures at 9.10 metres round. The other is a cedar of Lebanon whose lowest branches spread across the ground in a wide skirt of dark needles. Both came to us as readers' photographs.
meta_description: Two readers' trees near Clingoe Hill in Colchester: the Wivenhoe Whopper, a huge ancient oak, and a spreading cedar of Lebanon, and where they stand.

trees.name: The Oak of Clingoe Hill
trees.age_estimate: about 300 to 800 years, by readers' estimates
trees.story:
Locally this oak has a name, the Wivenhoe Whopper. It stands alone in open grass on Clingoe Hill in Greenstead, on the east side of Colchester, and the Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory records it as an ancient pedunculate oak with a girth of 9.10 metres at a height of 1.3 metres. Its recorder later noted a careful measurement of 8.57 metres and called it one of the biggest trees in Essex.

The inventory calls it a lapsed pollard, a tree once cut back above head height for its wood and then left to grow on. Readers' photographs show what that made. Under a full, rounded dome of leaves the trunk is short and enormously wide, with deep hollows and burrs at head height. In one, two people stand at its foot, one with arms spread against the bark, and they look small. The inventory lists a hollowing trunk, decaying wood in the crown, lichen and moss on the bark, and beefsteak fungus.

Nobody has dated it. One reader puts it at about 300 years; another, working from the Woodland Trust's guide to estimating the age of an oak from its girth, at about 800. Both are readers' estimates.

The inventory gives the ground as parkland and school or college land, with partial public access beside a footpath or road, so keep to the paths and follow any signs.

trees.name: The Cedar near Clingoe Hill

location.address: Near Clingoe Hill, Greenstead, Colchester, Essex

trees.story:
A couple of hundred metres from the great oak on Clingoe Hill, on the east side of Colchester, stands this cedar. It was sent to us by the same reader who photographed that oak in its autumn leaf, and they know it as a cedar of Lebanon.

Cedars of Lebanon have been planted in English parks since the seventeenth century, and given room they grow into one of the grandest shapes a tree can take. In the photograph the trunk divides low into several great limbs, and these sweep out and up in long curves, tier above tier, carrying flat dark plates of foliage. The lowest branches have come right down and spread across the ground, so the tree seems to stand in a pool of its own needles, with mown grass and a path beyond. A second picture shows a branch up close, short tufts of blue-green needles and pale green cones standing upright on the twigs like candles.

The reader came back with figures of their own, a girth of about 555 centimetres and an age of about 155 years by their estimate. We have found no survey or planting record to set beside them, so if you know its history, tell us here.

Walk round to where the low branches meet the grass and look up through the arches of the limbs.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad cedar whose trunk splits low into great curving limbs in tiers, its lowest branches lying along the ground in a wide skirt of dark needles, mown grass and a path behind it.
trees.access: The reader photographed it from mown grass beside a path. We found no published access terms for the ground, so follow any signs.

question_meta: A very large oak and a spreading cedar stand near Clingoe Hill in Colchester. Where they are and what readers say about them.
question_answer: A huge pedunculate oak (Quercus robur) stands on Clingoe Hill, Greenstead, Colchester. The Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory knows it as the Wivenhoe Whopper and records a girth of 9.10 metres; readers put it at about 300 to 800 years old.
question_context: Both trees on this page came to us as readers' photographs, sent through the app. The oak stands alone in open grass on Clingoe Hill in Greenstead, on the east side of Colchester; the first reader's own label placed it near Mistley, about ten kilometres away, so we have put it where it stands. A second reader pointed us to its record in the Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory, where it is the Wivenhoe Whopper: an ancient pedunculate oak and lapsed pollard with a girth of 9.10 metres at 1.3 metres, which its recorder later measured more carefully at 8.57 metres. Its photographs show a rounded crown over a short trunk with deep hollows and burrs at head height. Nobody has dated it; readers' estimates run from about 300 to about 800 years. A couple of hundred metres to the east, a reader photographed a cedar of Lebanon whose trunk splits low into curving limbs and whose lowest branches lie along the grass. The inventory lists partial public access beside a footpath or road for the oak, so keep to the paths. If you know a tree's history, tell us on its page and it goes into this answer.
